analysis.one_liner: Requires airlines to give stranded passengers food, water, and the right to leave a plane after three hours on the tarmac.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote; it sat in the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee for nearly two years until the Congress ended in January 2013.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would require every airline and airport to file a plan with the Transportation Department for handling planes stuck on the ground for long periods. Airlines would have to provide food, water, working restrooms, ventilation, and medical access to passengers on a delayed plane, and let them off after three hours on the tarmac. Airlines and airports that failed to follow their plans could be fined, the plans would be public, and a federal hotline would be created for passenger complaints.
analysis.who_benefits: Airline passengers stuck on planes that sit on the runway or at the gate for hours — they would get food, water, working restrooms, ventilation, medical access, and the option to get off the plane after three hours. Airlines that follow the rules would also gain a level regulatory playing field.

how_it_helps.text: Airlines would have to provide passengers on a grounded, delayed plane with adequate food, potable water, restrooms, cabin ventilation, and access to medical treatment.

After three hours on the tarmac before takeoff or after landing, passengers would have the option to deplane and return to the terminal, with this offered at least once every three hours that the plane stays on the ground, covering diverted flights too.
The Transportation Secretary could assess civil penalties against airlines or airports that fail to submit, get approval of, or follow their contingency plans, and the approved plans would be public.
Airports would have to describe in their plans how they will get passengers off delayed planes and share facilities and gates with delayed aircraft.
The Transportation Secretary would have to set up a consumer hotline telephone number for air passenger complaints.

analysis.who_pays: Airlines and airports, which would bear the cost of contingency planning, providing services during delays, and possible civil penalties. Some of those costs could be passed on to travelers through fares. The hotline would be paid for with federal appropriations.

drawbacks.text: The bill lets a pilot delay deplaning if they reasonably determine the plane will depart or unload within 30 minutes of the three-hour mark, or that deplaning would endanger safety or security — a safety exception that critics could argue swallows much of the guarantee.
Airlines and airports would face compliance costs and exposure to civil penalties for missing paperwork or failing to follow approved plans, costs that could partly show up in ticket prices.

A fixed three-hour deplaning rule can force airlines to return to the gate and cancel flights in situations where they might otherwise have gotten airborne shortly after, trading inconvenience on some flights for protection on others.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For passengers, the benefit is real: anyone who has sat on a closed plane for hours without water or a working restroom knows the problem. The costs to airlines are modest — much of this was already required by a Transportation Department regulation adopted in 2010, so the bill largely would have written that rule into law, added penalties, and extended obligations to airports. The main genuine trade-off is the cancellation risk from a firm three-hour clock, and the bill's own pilot exceptions blunt that. On balance, the protections for travelers outweigh the compliance burden, which is precisely why the airline industry preferred the matter stay with the lighter regulatory regime.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and then to its Aviation Subcommittee, and it never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the Congress ended in January 2013.

narrative.text: Rep. Mike Thompson of California introduced the bill on February 15, 2011, with 24 original cosponsors.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure the day it was introduced, and to that committee's Aviation Subcommittee the next day.
Thirty-five members cosponsored the bill — 32 Democrats and 3 Republicans — but the committee took no further action on it.
The bill sat without any hearing, markup, or vote for the remainder of the 112th Congress, which ended January 3, 2013.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Airlines and airports are better off because the bill died: they avoided a statutory mandate, public approved plans, and civil penalties layered on top of the existing Transportation Department rule. Travelers gained nothing beyond the protections they already had under that 2010 regulation.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Airlines and airports, which faced no new mandates

for.name: Rep. Mike Thompson
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 24 original cosponsors on the day of introduction.

against.name: Rep. John Mica
against.role: Chair, House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee
against.what_they_did: The committee he chaired took no action on the bill: no hearing, no markup, no vote; it was referred to the Aviation Subcommittee and stayed there until the Congress ended.

against.name: U.S. airline industry
against.role: Air carriers and their trade associations
against.what_they_did: Airline trade groups had fought the Transportation Department's 2010 tarmac-delay regulation, including in court, and opposed putting such requirements into statute, which would add fines and make the rules permanent law rather than something an administration could revise.

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship was overwhelmingly Democratic — 32 Democrats to 3 Republicans — and the bill died in the Republican-chaired committee without ever reaching the floor.

industries.note: The bill would require airlines to file government-approved tarmac contingency plans, provide food, water, restrooms, and medical access during long delays, let passengers off after three hours, file incident reports, and face civil penalties for noncompliance. Because a similar Department of Transportation regulation already existed, the practical effect was largely to lock the rule into law with fines attached, which is why carriers favored keeping it a lighter-touch regulation.

Airport operators would have to submit approved plans for deplaning passengers and for sharing gates and facilities with delayed aircraft, and could face civil penalties for failing to submit, obtain approval of, or follow those plans. Airlines already had obligations under the 2010 rule; this extended the mandate to a new set of businesses.
